title: Assignment: stack & queue problems
overview: This module is an assignment that puts stacks and queues to work. You compare the pop order of a stack and a queue (once with the STL, once with your own linked-list classes), cancel pairs of characters with a stack, and simulate a ticket line with a queue. The big lesson: pick the container whose removal order matches the problem.

concepts.explain: A stack gives back the **last** value you pushed (LIFO). A queue gives back the **first** value you pushed (FIFO). So pushing the same list into both gives opposite removal orders.
To check if two containers remove items in the same order, look at `top()` and `front()` together, compare, then pop both. Stop at the first mismatch.

When a new character can cancel the one just before it, keep the not-yet-cancelled characters on a stack. The top is always the 'previous available' character. If the stack is empty at the end, everything cancelled.
concepts.snippet:
if(!st.empty() && st.top()=='0' && c=='1') st.pop();
else st.push(c);

concepts.explain: A ticket line is a queue: join at the back with `push`, leave from the front with `front()` + `pop()`. Always check `empty()` before reading the front.
A doubly linked list with a `tail` pointer gives O(1) push/pop at the tail (a stack). A singly linked list with `head` and `tail` gives O(1) push at the tail and pop at the head (a queue).
If the two lists have different lengths, they can never be the same, so print `NO` right away. Read all input first, then decide.

files.title: Same or not (STL stack and queue)
files.what: Pushes `n` values into a `stack` and `m` values into a `queue`, then checks whether popping both gives the same sequence. Uses the STL containers.
steps: Read `n` and `m`, then push `n` values into `st` and `m` values into `q`.
If `n != m`, the lengths differ, so print `NO` and stop.
While `st` is not empty, compare `st.top()` with `q.front()`.
On any mismatch print `NO` and return; otherwise pop both and continue.
If the loop finishes, every pair matched, so print `YES`.
files.input_note: First line n and m, then the stack values, then the queue values.
files.output_note: `YES`: the stack pops 4 3 2 1, and the queue was filled with 4 3 2 1, so it also removes 4 3 2 1.
files.watch_out: The size check comes **after** reading both lines on purpose. If you returned before reading, it would not matter here, but in multi-test problems leftover input would break the next case.

check.q: If both lines are `1 2 3`, what is printed and why?
check.a: `NO`. The stack pops 3 first but the queue removes 1 first.

files.title: Same or not 2 (hand-made stack and queue)
files.what: Same task as problem 1, but without the STL: `myStack` (doubly linked list) and `myQueue` (singly linked list) are written by hand and used exactly like the STL ones.
steps: `Node` holds `val`, `next` and `prev`.
`myStack::push` adds at `tail`; `pop` deletes `tail` and moves `tail` back with `prev`; `top` returns `tail->val`.
`myQueue::push` adds at `tail`; `pop` deletes `head` and moves `head` forward; `front` returns `head->val`.
Both reset the other end to `NULL` when the list becomes empty, so the next push starts fresh.
`main` is the same as problem 1: read, check sizes, compare `top()` with `front()` while popping.
files.input_note: First line n and m, then the stack values, then the queue values.
files.output_note: `NO`: the first two pairs match (4 with 4, 3 with 3), but then the stack gives 2 while the queue gives 1.
files.watch_out: `myStack::pop` has no empty check. Calling it on an empty stack dereferences `NULL`. Here it is safe because `main` only pops while `!st.empty()`.

check.q: Why does the stack need a `prev` pointer but the queue does not?
check.a: The stack removes from the tail, so after deleting it must step back to the previous node. The queue removes from the head and only ever moves forward with `next`.

files.title: Is it valid? (cancel 01 and 10 pairs)
files.what: A `0` can delete a previous `1` and a `1` can delete a previous `0`. The string is valid if everything gets deleted. A stack keeps the characters still alive.
steps: Read `t` test cases; for each, read the string `s` and start an empty `stack<char>`.
For every character `c`: if the stack is empty, push it.
Otherwise, if `c` and `st.top()` are different digits, they cancel, so pop.
If they are the same digit, push `c`.
After the loop, an empty stack means `YES`, else `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(|s|) per test · Space O(|s|)
files.input_note: First line t, then one binary string per line.
files.output_note: `YES YES NO` (one per line). In `0001` the three 0s pile up and only one of them is cancelled by the final 1.
files.watch_out: Because any different pair cancels, the answer is simply 'the number of 0s equals the number of 1s'. The stack still shows the general pattern.

check.q: Trace `0110`: what does the stack hold after each character?

files.title: Special queries (ticket line)
files.what: Simulates a ticket counter line with a `queue<string>`. Command `0 name` adds a person; command `1` serves the front person or prints `Invalid` if the line is empty.
steps: Read the number of queries `n` and create `queue<string> q`.
For each query read `x`.
If `x == 0`, read a name and `push` it to the back.
If `x == 1` and the queue is empty, print `Invalid`.
Otherwise print `q.front()` and `pop` it.
files.input_note: First line q, then one command per line.
files.output_note: `Invalid`, `rina`, `tomal`, `Invalid`: the first and last `1` find an empty line; the middle two serve people in the order they joined.
files.watch_out: Never call `front()` on an empty queue: it is undefined behaviour. The `empty()` check must come first.

check.q: Why is a queue (not a stack) right for this problem?
check.a: People are served in the order they arrived: first in, first out.

files.title: Elimination (every 1 removes a 0 just before it)
files.what: Only the pair `01` (a 0 followed by a 1) gets eliminated, and eliminations keep chaining. A stack handles the chaining automatically.
steps: For each test, read `s` and start an empty `stack<char>`.
If the stack is empty, push `c` and move on.
If `st.top() == '0'` and `c == '1'`, the pair `01` disappears, so pop.
Otherwise push `c` (this includes a `0` after a `1`, which does **not** cancel).
Empty stack at the end → `YES`, else `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(|s|) per test · Space O(|s|)
files.input_note: First line t, then one binary string per line.
files.output_note: `YES`, `NO`, `YES`. `10` stays because a 0 cannot remove the 1 before it.
files.watch_out: Compare with problem 3: there both `01` and `10` cancel. Here only `01` does, so the order of characters matters, not just the counts.

check.q: Does `0101` become empty? Show the stack.

recap: Stack = last in, first out; queue = first in, first out.
To compare two containers, check the fronts/tops together and pop both.
A stack is the natural tool for 'cancel with the previous available item' problems, including chain reactions.
A hand-made stack and queue are just linked lists with the right end pointers.

check_yourself.q: You push 1 2 3 into a stack and 3 2 1 into a queue. Are they 'same'?
check_yourself.a: Yes. The stack pops 3 2 1 and the queue removes 3 2 1.

check_yourself.q: Why does a stack handle chained eliminations like `0011` without extra loops?
check_yourself.a: After a pair is removed, the new top is the character that now sits just before the next one, so the next comparison is automatically against it.

check_yourself.q: What is the time cost of push and pop in the linked-list stack and queue?
check_yourself.a: O(1) each, because they only touch the head or tail pointer.
